utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will the registrar call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-04-81-PT, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And may we have the appearances.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, and good afternoon, Your Honour. For the Prosecution, Susan Somers. To my left, Ms. Carmela Javier, case manager; to my right, Mr. Frederic Ossogo, trial attorney; and Mr. Rafael La Cruz, legal officer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: James Castle, appearing on behalf of Momcilo Perisic. Appearing with me is Tina Drolec. And our client is on provisional release at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a Status Conference in respect of the case Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic, and its purpose is to organise exchanges between the parties to ensure the expeditious preparation of the trial. We'll also look at the status of the case and hear from the accused, if necessary. I begin first, Ms. Somers, with disclosure under Rule 66(A)(i), supporting material to the indictment, and recall at the last Status Conference the disclosure was complete except for one document, which was subject to Rule 70 restrictions. Can you update me on that, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the situation is the same. It is complete except for that one document, and we are seeking some way perhaps to find the same document through a non-Rule 70 source. At this point, though, I cannot report further. But it is being worked on by the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I also recall that the Defence had requested re-disclosure of certain tapes that were of poor quality.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Accomplished, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That has been done?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Turn now to 66(A)(ii), witness statements. What is the position with regard to your witness statements, Ms. Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has not put forth a preliminary witness list. However, pursuant to directions of the Chamber from the last Status Conference, we indicated -- for purposes of prospective 92 bis, 89(F) witnesses, we supplied a list from -- they're principally crime based and some expert witnesses. From the standpoint of viva voce or additional witnesses, we have not put forth a list. It was discussed yesterday, Your Honour, at the 65 ter conference, and the Prosecution is prepared to formulate, subject to addition/revision, such a list if that would be of assistance without the direction of -- from the Chamber. But we can also embellish upon the suggestions that came from our 92 bis, 89(F) list, given that the crime bases, as Your Honour is aware, derive from the other cases, namely from Srebrenica, from Sarajevo, and from the Zagreb shelling which is reflected in the ongoing Martic case. There will be transcript evidence also from that latter case that we will have to examine. The -- if that would be of assistance and satisfactory, then we are prepared to go ahead and from that list work -- I think any 66(A)(ii) list that we would formulate now would of necessity be subject to revision with contacting of witnesses, also subject possibly to some agreement. We have -- as Your Honour is aware, we have sat down and attempted to iron out some points of agreement, and if we are able to continue to work at that pace, and I think we may be able to by the next --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe matters are at the stage where perhaps they should be more formalised. Mr. Castle?

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In addition to a list of the witnesses, I believe the Rule also calls for the production of witness statements and that is of concern to us, and if I can, I'll explain why. Originally in reviewing the 66(A)(i) submissions, there were a number of witnesses identified, at least in those materials. I believe the number was -- I can tell the Court what the number was. There were 58 witnesses identified in those materials. Then we received the 92 bis, 89(F) document by the Prosecution that announced a number of other witnesses; I believe it was total of 163. Only 11 of the witnesses that were in the original materials were reflected in this later list of 163 witnesses, and of the 163 witnesses that were in the 89(F), 92 bis document we did searches for statements, and only 53 of those witnesses were we able to find statements, either in -- on the EDS system, or in the materials that were specifically disclosed to the Defence. Keeping in mind that we don't have a trial date but a trial date can occur and come up on a scheduling docket fairly quickly, given a number of circumstances that we have no control over, I want to try to be prepared for trial as soon as I can, and the first step of that is to know who the Prosecution's witnesses are and to be able to review the statements of those witnesses. This becomes even more important later on when we're talking about experts, but I'll defer on that issue. The other matter that the Prosecution raised was the contacting of witnesses, and we have an agreement that any witnesses that they list we will not contact until such time as we notify the Prosecution of whatever provisions can be taken that seem to be necessary for that witness. And we have done that on a cooperative basis with the Prosecution at this point. I believe that addresses the issues raised by the Court and by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Castle. I'm going to make an order, Ms. Somers, requiring the Prosecution to provide copies of the statements of all witnesses that the Prosecutor intends to call to testify at trial, and this includes 92 bis and 89(F) witnesses and copies of all written statements. And this should be provided by Friday, the 18th of August. I turn next to Rule 68, exculpatory material.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, may I -- I'll comment on the date. Is the Chamber in a position to extend it a bit beyond that vacation period, if it's not too difficult or -- that would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is beyond the vacation. Because the vacation ends on the first week in August. I had that in mind, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And if this witness list, the Chamber has said "all." Clearly it may have -- we may have to request either extensions for -- not so much extensions but revisions of it. We'll do that in the appropriate manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sufficient until the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us deal with that if and when it arrives. Ms. Somers, Rule 68 exculpatory material.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We have our continuing obligations as we are aware, and we believe ourselves to be in compliance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Castle, anything on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: Your Honour, in our discussions yesterday it appears if we have a difference of opinion not in the obligation to provide 68 -- Rule 68 material but in the manner in which that is provided, it is our position that that has to be provided to us specifically and identified as such by the Prosecution, and we find authority in that in the practice directive issued by the President that stated so. The Prosecutor's office, their position is that Rule 68 material can be disclosed by its presence on the EDS system, which contains some five million documents. I believe that this issue is important enough that I had indicated to the Prosecution that I would file a pleading shortly addressing this issue, so they have an opportunity to address it. But it is our position, very briefly, that to have us look for it in a sea of documents of five million, some of which are not searchable because they're maybe handwritten or in a format that's not recognised by search engines is not a sufficient performance of the Prosecutor's obligations under Rule 68.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So, Ms. Somers, you take the position then that exculpatory material can be provided in electronic form on the EDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think my learned counsel opposite me have simplified a little bit the position. The discussion yesterday was whether it was 68(i) or (ii).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Or (ii), yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Right. And we were discussing (ii), 68(ii).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Oh, you're discussing (ii).

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: 68(ii), right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because that just deals with relevant material.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Principally 68(ii). And there have been -- I think it is less than clear, and Mr. Castle did send me a communication today indicating he wants to discuss or hear from us on it. And if the Chamber is minded to give us time to try to discuss this rather than make it an issue before the Court now, I would be appreciative, because if there is some misunderstanding about how we're doing it, it would be probably more convenient to have it worked out between the parties right now. But we have provided enormous quantities of material since our last conference, most of it referenced through the EDS and falling either under 66(B) or 68(ii). But again, unless there is a need today to get into it, and we do distinguish between the two provisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, there is a distinction.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But be careful that you wouldn't be using the provisions of 68(ii) to avoid the requirements of 68(i). It already wouldn't be presenting a sea of material in which there might be exculpatory material under 68(ii) when, in fact, it should be presented under 68(i). Mr. Castle, what are we talking about, 68(i) or 68(ii)?

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: It was my understanding it was the 68(i), which was the exculpatory material, and I do recognise there's a distinction, because 68(ii) specifically states it can be done in electronic form, whereas 68(i) does not so allow. And I think that the way that we can resolve this is I would like the opportunity to discuss this with the Prosecution, and if there is a disagreement, then perhaps we will raise it by motion. But what I would like to see is that 68(i) material that is exculpatory is identified as such and provided to us specifically, and 68(ii) material is something separate and can be done electronically. But I sympathise with the Prosecution. I did not raise this with them until yesterday and I, in all fairness, would like to give them an opportunity to resolve this with me, if there is a difference of understanding about what was said yesterday and give the parties an opportunity to try to resolve this without the Court's intervention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, then, try and resolve it, and if you can't, then perhaps you will file a motion. I understand that the Defence invoked Rule 66(B). That doesn't give rise to any issues? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. I turn next then to expert reports. There is some confusion about the number of expert witnesses, Ms. Somers, that you propose to rely on. Would you clarify that, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, at the last conference, I think that I myself had to check into the numbers, but the submission that we made to the Chamber on some of the 92 bis matters indicate that there are expert reports from the component cases that we would -- I have listed them, that we would seek to introduce by way of 92 bis. And they're from Galic, they will be from Dragomir Milosevic, perhaps, if they have additional experts, and the Srebrenica cases, as well as Martic. The substantive case on perhaps what might be called -- I don't want to use the term "linkage" with command and control experts, but there are two command and control experts engaged by the Prosecution, and I am not in a position to have reports filed yet, but those are the two that Mr. Castle has referred to. He is aware of who they are. And there are additionally some -- I don't want to use the term "summary," but some contextual expert opinion we will be seeking, not unlike that which has been used in some of the major cases before the Tribunal, for background and context. So the numbers reflect those from the other cases, particularly the forensic evidence. I have indicated to counsel that we would not seek to reprove, in essence, the forensics or -- unless there are specific issues. And they're demographics. There have been historical experts that we think are helpful for this case. And we have provided a couple of names so that the -- so that Mr. Castle can have a look through the JDB on the reports, and certainly as the list is more formalised, the actual reports, but that is how they are enumerated, both from the cases that go into the Perisic case and the necessary ones from the issues of command and control or the military aspects and context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Castle.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Our -- we had filed a status report with the Court that expressed some of our concerns with regards to experts. This case will be an expert-intensive case, perhaps not in the numbers hopefully, but in the terms of their importance to the findings of the Tribunal. Most importantly is the two experts that have been identified as command and control experts. I believe there was -- it was misspoken that their names had been provided to us, because we have not received their names, but if those names are to be provided, that is only one part of the problem. The other part of the problem is getting the reports, because in order for us to prepare our experts, to even employ our own experts, to know what kind of experts to hire, we have to know what it is the Prosecution is presenting. Because the Defence, in essence, reacts to the evidence that's presented against the defendant. And so the sooner that we can be presented with those reports, the better off we are in our ability to prepare and be ready for trial. And so we ask for this now, because we don't want to request delay later. With regards to the second kind of experts, which are the ones that were listed in the 89(F), 92 bis recent filing, recently, and I think yesterday, the Prosecution provided us with references to some of the expert reports that we were able to obtain. I still think there are some outstanding, but it sounds like it shouldn't take very long at all, because these experts have been used in the past and have produced reports in the past for not only their identities but their reports to be turned over to the Defence. I have to tell the Court that the EDS system does not contain expert reports. Those reports are sometimes on the joint database, because they've been admitted in other cases, but they're not on the EDS. And so it's our request that these experts be identified and that their reports be tendered, so that the Defence can be prepared in a reasonable time period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Castle. Again -- Yes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I know time and memory and obligations maybe have intervened, but in correspondence to our office on the 26th of October, 2005, and I'll keep it not in the record, but in paragraph 4, counsel has indicated that he is aware of who the experts are. They're named actually in the correspondence, so perhaps there has just been an oversight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, in any event, I think we are at a stage where it is appropriate for me to make an order requiring the Prosecutor to provide the reports of any expert witnesses to be called, and the date that I will fix for this is Friday, September the 29th.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I should have spoken before you made your -- if I may request that it may be perhaps into October because of who these individuals are, commitments, I must check them, and I'm happy to report back to the Chamber, but I need to make sure that I don't commit to something that I cannot deliver on. I know I want your order to be one that I can deliver. So may I -- within the next days I will speak to these individuals and confirm that that is doable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I will extend it by three weeks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And which date would that make it, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That would take us to -- September 29th. Friday, the 20th of October.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, on the -- on the -- what I will call summary of witnesses, I may make a separate submission on time-frame because it -- I have spoken to the in-house personnel who would be involved, and I want to make sure that -- and I just added this yesterday, I just spoke of this for the first time to the Defence, so I want to make sure that I can get an indication from them as to their time-frame, and I will also, if it's not possible within here, within this time limit, I will so notify or request as to those individuals, an extension. But as to the others, I -- I appreciate the extension to October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. So that's Friday, October the 20th. Pre-trial preparation, and Rule 92 bis and 89(F) evidence. The order that I made earlier is comprehensive enough to cover those matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, what we had done is we made it the first -- the initial report and there will be additions to that as we go through the materials, so that we're trying to keep the live testimony to a minimum and then the appropriate motions will be made. But as I indicated, it was sort of first report, if that's satisfactory, as some of those come up. Because there will be people added to the list you will get that were not indicated on the first, and that's because it was an initial report based on the proposed use of those two Rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Nothing on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the position, Ms. Somers first, on the question of adjudicated facts and agreed facts? You did comply with the order which I made the last time to provide a report within two months on -- on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We did, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the status of the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I think a bit frozen. We've spent two full good working days together, and our view is that there are -- for certain points of agreement, there certainly is adequate material, and the Defence takes a different perspective on it. And what we submitted to the Chamber reflects where we stand and that either -- I think we just showed position modified and it can reflect either we've lost ground on some of where we thought we were, or we've gained it. But I was informed yesterday that counsel would -- and I should let him speak for himself, but that until there is more information, initially I think it was the concept of disclosure, yesterday I believe the term was statements. We're not -- we don't seem to be able to move very far. But I will, nevertheless, if we cannot reach agreement I will make a motion at the appropriate time for the -- or request for the admission of certain adjudicated facts. I also am hopeful that before this trial starts we will have benefit of the Galic decision, which would be very useful, I think, in this case, and any other pending Srebrenica matters that will be helpful. So ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Castle.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I agree in part and disagree in part with the statements of opposing counsel. We have now 158.000 pages of disclosure materials that were specifically disclosed to the Defence. Over 125.000 of that was given since the last Status Conference. As hard as we can work, it is impossible for us to get through in three months' period of time. A lot of the agreed upon facts as stated are allegations -- literally what it is is a list of the parts of the indictment broken down, and the indictment was written in a very argumentative and conclusory fashion, and so a lot of those facts we cannot agree to, and there is going to be a problem with that. With that said, where I see substantial opportunity for agreement is in the stipulation to the admission of transcripts perhaps, statements made by witnesses, expert reports, things of that nature, that we don't have yet or we haven't had the opportunity to review yet. What those reports mean, however, I believe are subject to interpretation and argument. And that is where I want to preserve on behalf of my client the ability to argue at trial, because an indictment, by its nature, is argumentative. It's arguing for a position and for a conclusion and because of that it's often written in a fashion that's really not agreeable by both sides, whereas the constituent facts that the Prosecution relies upon for that -- for a particular portion of the indictment can be stipulated to and still allow the Defence to argue that it has a different conclusion. And I can give the Court an example. In the indictment it indicates that there was essentially a lot of intelligence information that would give our client the knowledge that war crimes had been committed by certain individuals that are named as subordinates. What the disclosure shows, on the other hand, is that there are reports, and nowhere in those reports that we've received is there any indication of any war crimes. So the conclusion that the Prosecution draws in its indictment, that this information showed knowledge, we can't agree to. But we may very well be able to agree to the admission of these intelligence reports themselves. And that's just one example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's fair enough. I don't think they could be expecting you to agree to something as essential as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: What we have talked to them about is stipulating to the admission of exhibits, and that these exhibits are the way that we would prefer to proceed as opposed to the conclusions that can be drawn from those exhibits. And so I believe there is room for substantial progress in this regard, and we're happy to sit down with it, with the Prosecution and discuss this. Today or this time period was a bit premature for us to make any substantial progress on because we frankly have limited resources with which to review these documents. And what we're trying to work with the Prosecution is for them, at some point, we're not asking for any Court intervention at this time, to give us a list of the documents that they wish us to stipulate for admission, or statements, or expert reports and look to see if we can stipulate to those. And the ones that we don't, then perhaps there is an 89(F), 92 bis motion that can be filed by the Prosecution and we can litigate its admissibility. But that's the way the Defence prefers to proceed. And I believe, once again, we can make substantial progress in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is a criminal trial and what I expect from both parties is a good-faith effort to try to narrow the issues down as much as possible. I've considered the question of setting a time for the filing of the pre-trial briefs, but I still believe it is not the right time yet to make such an order. And so I keep that matter under consideration. The next Status Conference has to be held before Friday, the 13th of October. And I would set Wednesday, the 4th of October as the date for the next conference. Do you have other matters to raise? Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I don't, sir. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Castle.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The hearing is adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at
